newsitem.title: GERMANY: Canadian officials meet in Germany on Zaire aid.
newsitem.headline: Canadian officials meet in Germany on Zaire aid.

text.p: Canadian military leaders met on Friday with officials from some 40 countries and non-government organisations to shape a planned military mission to aid hundreds of thousands of refugees in Zaire and Rwanda.

Officials said the meeting at the U.S. European Command headquarters was not expected to make any decision on whether to send a force after countries meeting in New York on Wednesday renewed support for a mission but only if necessary.
"We are here to discuss the military aspects of the operation," said Lieutenant Colonel Rejan Duchesneau, a spokesman for the Canadian military at the Stuttgart meeting.
Duchesneau declined to say how long the meeting would last. "It will take as long as it takes," he said.
A news conference was scheduled to be held after the meeting at Kelley Barracks.

Britain, France and Spain have all said the force was still required despite the return of hundreds of thousands of refugees to Rwanda in the last week, because several hundred thousand refugees are still believed to be in Zaire.
Zaire has also maintained that a multinational force is still needed to help refugees and displaced Zaireans. It also wants such a force to help it recovery territory from rebels.

But Washington, stung by the failure of its Somali military mission in the early 1990s, has cancelled plans to send combat troops to the region and instead has begun preparing for an airlift in which the U.S. military would provide logistics.
Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said in Ottawa on Thursday that the Stuttgart meeting would not take any decisions on whether to send a multinational force to central Africa.
"There will not be a decision in Stuttgart. It is a meeting to look at all the factors and all the options, and after that there will be a context for a decision," Axworthy said.
Asked when a decision would be made on how to proceed with the Canadian-led rescue mission, he said: "Soon... We'll make the decision when we can."
Several African nations -- including Zimbabwe, Botswana, Cameroon, Senegal and South Africa -- were present at the talks as well as representatives from several major Western powers.

Military leaders in Stuttgart were expected to pore over the latest reports from the region, including information from reconnaissance flights to determine the region's needs after the exodus last week of half a million refugees to Rwanda.
Since last Friday, Hutu refugees have begun streaming into Rwanda, causing some nations, especially the United States, to question the need to put ground troops in eastern Zaire.

Hundreds of thousands of Huto refugees have fled back into Rwanda to escape fighting between Zairean Tutsi rebels, supported by Rwanda, and soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated ex-army and militias, who organised the 1994 Rwandan genocide of minority Tutsis.

Aid organisation officials have begun to express alarm at the possibility that the multinational force might not even go to Zaire and Rwanda, noting that many refugees were still cut off and unable to cross the border.

"We need to create humanitarian corridors, safe haven and delivery mechanisms to reach these people, and we need the help of the Canadian-led forces to do it," CARE Canada, one of the agencies mandated to distribute aid in Africa, said on Thursday.
